title: Best Indian Property Markets for NRI Buyers in 2026: A City-by-City Guide
excerpt: From Hyderabad's record appreciation to Bangalore's unmatched rental yields, a breakdown of where diaspora investors are putting their money and what's changed this year.
body:
• NRIs account for 18–22% of primary residential sales across India's eight largest cities, with roughly 60% of that investment originating in Gulf Cooperation Council countries.
  • Hyderabad leads on capital appreciation at 22–28% over two years while Bangalore offers the highest rental yields at 4–6%, making both standout picks for diaspora buyers in 2026.
  • A recent Equirus Wealth survey of 8,300 Gulf-based NRIs found 40% are actively reducing their Indian real estate allocation — the highest negative sentiment across any asset class — in favour of equities and mutual funds.
  • Geopolitical tensions in the Gulf and airspace disruptions have slowed property deal closures as buyers adopt a wait-and-watch stance, though inquiries remain strong.

For millions of Non-Resident Indians, buying property back home remains one of the most emotionally charged financial decisions they make. It is part investment, part insurance, part identity — a stake in a country many left but never stopped calling home. In 2026, with the rupee under pressure, Indian real estate prices climbing, and Gulf geopolitics adding a layer of urgency, the calculus is shifting fast.

Where the Smart Money Is Going

The Indian residential market has emerged from the pandemic-era reset with clear winners and losers for NRI buyers. Industry data and property advisory firms point to five cities that dominate diaspora investment, each offering a distinct risk-return profile.

Gurgaon remains the premium play. Prices range from ₹12,000 to ₹35,000 per square foot across corridors like Dwarka Expressway and Golf Course Road, with rental yields of 3.5–5.2% and two-year appreciation of 18–25%. The city benefits from proximity to Delhi's international airport and a deep bench of corporate tenants, though stamp duty at 7–8% is among the highest in the country.

Bangalore offers the strongest rental income story. India's tech capital delivers yields of 4–6% — the highest among major cities — with prices at ₹7,000–22,000 per square foot. Whitefield, Sarjapur Road, and Hebbal attract a reliable stream of tech-sector tenants, making it the preferred market for NRIs seeking steady cash flow. Buyers should verify BBMP approvals and flood-risk assessments in some pockets.

Hyderabad is the value play with the best appreciation track record. Prices at ₹6,000–16,000 per square foot are significantly more affordable than Gurgaon or Mumbai, yet premium corridors in HITECH City, Gachibowli, and Kokapet have delivered 22–28% appreciation over 2022–2025 — the fastest in the country. This is the "buy early" market for NRIs willing to bet on continued IT-sector expansion.

Pune occupies the middle ground. At ₹6,500–14,000 per square foot with 3–4.2% yields and 12–16% appreciation, it is less volatile than Gurgaon and cheaper than Bangalore. The Hinjewadi-Wakad tech corridor and Kharadi attract steady demand.

Mumbai remains the trophy market. Prices start at ₹15,000 per square foot and climb past ₹60,000 in South Mumbai and Worli, with relatively modest yields of 2.5–3.5%. The entry budget is ₹2 crore and up. Mumbai property is a long-term wealth play rather than an income play — but for many NRIs, especially those from Maharashtra, the emotional pull overrides pure financial logic.

The Gulf NRI Shift

A notable behavioural change is underway among the largest bloc of NRI property buyers. An April 2026 survey by Equirus Wealth, covering over 8,300 GCC-based NRI clients, found that 40% are actively reducing their allocation to Indian real estate — the sharpest negative sentiment recorded across any asset class. Meanwhile, 73% are increasing exposure to Indian equities and mutual funds.

"There is a noticeable change in how buyers are approaching real estate today. The conversation has moved beyond price cycles to long-term value."

— Ankush Kaul, President of Sales, Central Park

The shift reflects growing financial sophistication among Gulf NRIs, many of whom are pivoting from illiquid physical assets toward more organised and liquid financial products. Investment and retirement planning now rival traditional family support as the primary purpose of remittances, according to the survey.

Geopolitical tensions have added friction. With airspace disruptions and Iran-related security concerns roiling the Gulf, some buyers are deferring site visits and property registrations. Developers report that inquiries remain strong, but deal closures have lengthened as buyers adopt a wait-and-watch posture.

What NRI Buyers Need to Know

The legal framework for NRI property purchases in India is well-established under FEMA. NRIs and OCI cardholders can buy residential and commercial properties without special RBI approval, provided payments are routed through NRE or NRO accounts. Agricultural land, plantations, and farmhouses remain off-limits.

Key considerations for 2026 buyers include verifying RERA registration for under-construction projects, budgeting for stamp duty (4–7% depending on state) plus 1% registration, and arranging a Power of Attorney for transactions that require physical presence. Sale proceeds from NRE-funded purchases are fully repatriable, while rental income from NRO accounts can be repatriated up to $1 million per financial year after taxes, with Forms 15CA and 15CB from a chartered accountant.

The India-UK free trade pact that took effect this month and the RBI's recent decision to raise investment limits for NRIs and OCIs in Indian equities both point to a policy environment that is becoming more, not less, welcoming to diaspora capital. For NRIs sitting on Gulf dirhams or US dollars, the question is no longer whether to invest in India — it is where, when, and how much.
